nameStory: This magnificent cat has collected names like a world traveler collecting passport stamps! 'Mountain lion' comes from its preference for rocky, mountainous terrain, while 'cougar' derives from the Brazilian Tupi word 'çuçuarana.' Other regional names include puma, panther, and catamount (short for 'cat of the mountain'), making it one of the most alias-heavy animals in North America.
description: The mountain lion is a large, powerful wild cat about the size of a big dog, weighing 80-200 pounds with males being significantly larger than females. Picture a house cat scaled up dramatically - it has the same graceful build but with incredible muscle mass, especially in the shoulders and hindquarters. Its solid-colored coat ranges from tawny brown to grayish, without spots or stripes like other wild cats. With only 2 confirmed observations in New England, encountering one would be extraordinarily rare.

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: Massive cat with a lean, muscular build - think oversized house cat with the proportions of a linebacker. Adults are typically 6-8 feet long including the tail, standing about 2 feet at the shoulder.

idTips.label: Fur
idTips.description: Short, dense coat that feels coarse to the touch, uniformly colored in tawny brown, gray-brown, or silvery-gray. No spots, stripes, or patterns - just solid color throughout with lighter undersides.

idTips.label: Tracks
idTips.description: Large round paw prints about 3-4 inches across with four toes and no claw marks (cats retract their claws). Tracks show a distinctive asymmetrical pattern with the leading toe clearly ahead of the others.

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves with fluid, silent grace and incredible stealth. Typically solitary and extremely elusive, active mainly at dawn and dusk. May freeze motionless when spotted rather than immediately fleeing.

idTips.label: Sign
idTips.description: Scat is segmented and rope-like, about 1 inch thick, often containing hair and bone fragments. May find scratch marks on trees 6-10 feet high where they mark territory.

habitat: In the extremely rare chance you'd encounter one in New England, it would likely be in remote, heavily forested mountainous areas with dense underbrush and rocky outcroppings. They prefer terrain that offers plenty of cover for stalking prey, particularly areas with healthy deer populations. Look for habitat that connects to larger wilderness corridors, as these cats require enormous territories.

seasonality.spring: Most active during dawn and dusk hours as prey becomes more active. This is breeding season, so males may travel greater distances and be slightly more visible.
seasonality.summer: Primarily nocturnal during hot weather, seeking cool rocky dens and shaded areas during the day. Young may be born and hidden in secluded rocky caves or dense thickets.
seasonality.fall: Increased activity as they build up fat reserves for winter and prey species are most abundant. May be spotted more often during daylight hours.
seasonality.winter: Grow thick winter coats that appear more grayish. Follow prey species to lower elevations and may be more active during warmer midday periods.

funFact: A mountain lion can leap 40 feet horizontally from a standstill and jump 15 feet straight up into a tree - that's like jumping from the ground onto a two-story roof in a single bound!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with a very large dog or possibly a black bear at a distance, but the long, thick tail (nearly half the body length) and distinctly feline gait are dead giveaways. Remember: if the tail is as long as the body, it's definitely a cat, not a dog or bear.
contextualKnowledge: Mountain lions were historically native to New England but were eliminated by hunting and habitat loss by the early 1900s. Today's rare sightings are likely dispersing individuals from established western populations, not a breeding population. Many reported 'mountain lion' sightings turn out to be large house cats, dogs, or other animals seen under poor lighting conditions.
compareHints: As the only wild cat of its size in North America, mountain lions are unmistakable when seen clearly. Unlike lynx or bobcats (much smaller wild cats), mountain lions lack ear tufts, have long tails instead of short 'bobbed' ones, and are much more heavily built. Their solid coat color distinguishes them from spotted cats like ocelots or jaguars found elsewhere in the Americas.
